Metrology and Inspection, stage 7 of 15Next stage: 08 Transistors and the Front End

In plain terms

Metrology (measurement) and inspection are a chip factory's quality control. Between the steps that build a chip, another machine looks the wafer over. It checks whether the lines are the right width, whether this layer landed squarely on the last one, and whether a speck of dirt has killed a circuit. The main chip in an AI accelerator, the one that does the calculating, is one of the largest cut from a wafer. A bigger chip is a bigger target for a speck. On a chip that size, halving the stray specks lifts the share of flawless chips from about half to about seven in ten. In 2025 one American firm, KLA, held about five times the market share of its nearest rival. So a chip factory, or fab, cut off from KLA would find fewer of the faults that make its chips fail.

In short

Chipmakers use inspection and measurement tools to find defects and raise the share of chips that work. KLA, the world's leading supplier of these tools, sells to every major chipmaker[2]. CSET, a Georgetown University research center, puts KLA at 56.8 percent of this market in 2025, about five times Applied Materials, the next largest supplier[1]. Since October 2022, US rules have required a license for any US tool, inspection tools included, bound for China's most advanced fabs[20]. A December 2024 rule added specific inspection and measurement tools to the export control list, including those that find defects 21 nm across or smaller[21]. The rule calls that size critical for advanced chips[21].

Why substitution is possible
Metrology and inspection tools measure and inspect wafers so a fab can find and fix faults in its process. KLA is the biggest maker, but eight other firms each hold more than 1 percent of the market. Applied Materials and Hitachi each lead at least one kind of tool. A fab that loses KLA and buys from the others keeps running. But it finds fewer flaws and fixes them more slowly. A country barred from buying from any of them has to rely on its own makers. Chinese firms held 0.7 percent of the market for these tools in 2025 by CSET's count.
Where China stands

Chinese makers are still small in metrology and inspection, but one of them is growing fast. CSET's count, built on TechInsights data, puts all Chinese firms at 0.7 percent of the market for these tools in 2025, against 0.2 percent of lithography tools. Skyverse, a Shenzhen maker of inspection and metrology tools, reported 2.05 billion yuan of revenue in 2025, about $285 million and up 48.75 percent on 2024. Skyverse's revenue alone is about 1.8 percent of CSET's market, so the CSET count may miss some domestic sales. In its 2025 annual report Skyverse says Chinese makers still hold a low share of China's own market for these tools, where KLA holds the largest share. CSET's July 2025 survey of Chinese share gains from 2019 to 2024 covers deposition, etch, polishing, lithography, packaging and test, but leaves out measurement and inspection.

Where the US stands

KLA is the largest maker of metrology and inspection tools in the world. CSET's Supply Chain Explorer puts it at 56.8 percent of the 2025 market, about five times Applied Materials. Citing Gartner, KLA puts its 2024 share at 56.5 percent, or 6.5 times its nearest rival. In 2025 American firms held 71.7 percent of this market and Japanese firms 14.1 percent. Since October 2022 the US has required a license for any US tool bound for China's most advanced fabs. A December 2024 US rule added specific metrology and inspection tools to the export control list. It names defect inspection tools that find defects 21 nm across or smaller, high-accuracy overlay and wafer shape metrology, and film and line-width metrology for non-planar transistors.

See it in 3D in the interactive chapter

Process control tools, the machines that measure and inspect wafers, were a $15.7 billion market in 2025[1]. KLA puts the whole wafer equipment market, including advanced packaging, at about $120 billion that year[2].

CSET's count for 2025, built on TechInsights data, puts KLA at 56.8 percent, about five times Applied Materials' 11.2 percent[1]. At its March 2026 investor day KLA cited Gartner's figures for 2024, which put its share at 56.5 percent, 6.5 times its nearest competitor[3]. In April 2026 KLA said its 2025 share was about 7 times the nearest competitor's[4]. The figures use different data and years, so KLA's lead over the next firm ranges from about 5 to about 7 times.

How it works

An inspection tool sweeps a beam of light across the wafer, photographs it, and compares the image of each chip with the image of its neighbors. The chips on a wafer are meant to be identical, so anything that shows in one and not the others is a defect. The tool records where each defect is. For faults too small for light to show, a second tool scans a beam of electrons across a small patch and builds a picture from the electrons that bounce back.

A metrology tool measures known shapes. It shines light on a test pattern printed beside the circuits and works out from the scattered light how wide the lines are and how thick the film is. It also reads marks printed in this layer and the last to measure how far the two are out of line, which chipmakers call overlay.

The fab pays for all this to protect yield, the share of chips on a wafer that work. A wafer loses value two ways: whole regions ruined by mishandling, misalignment or over-etching, and single circuits killed by stray material or an airborne particle[5].

A bigger chip is a bigger target for the second kind, and the loss grows faster than the area. Chipmakers call each chip on a wafer a die. In the standard formula, die yield is (1 + D0A/a) to the power minus a. Here D0 is defects per square centimeter, A is die area, and a is a clustering constant of 3 to 4 that says how much defects bunch together. At a defect density of 0.8 per square centimeter, with a set to 3, a 1 square centimeter die yields 49.2 percent and a 2 by 2 centimeter die 11.3 percent[5]. Because the bigger die yields less and fits fewer times on a wafer, it costs 20.1 times as much as the small one[5].

By the same formula, an 8 square centimeter die, about as much as one exposure can print, yields about 49 percent at 0.10 defects per square centimeter, with a set to 3[5]. Halving the defect density to 0.05 lifts that yield to about 69 percent[5]. Engineers move a fab from the first figure to the second by finding the process step that is losing dies and fixing it, work called yield learning.

Those percentages are the share of dies with no killer defect. A chip built from many identical blocks can carry spares and switch off a faulty block[5]. Nvidia's full H100 design has 144 of its main computing blocks, called streaming multiprocessors, and the SXM5 version it ships has 132 turned on[6]. So the share of dies that can be sold is higher than the formula gives. But the formula shows how fast flawless dies get scarce as chips grow.

Variants and trade-offs

The tools trade sensitivity against speed. All the market sizes and shares below are CSET's, for 2025[1].

  • Defect inspection scans a whole wafer with light or electrons and compares each die against its neighbors. It is by far the largest family, at $6.7 billion, and KLA held 85.9 percent of it. ASML's HMI eScan 1100 runs 25 electron beams at once, up to 15 times the throughput of single-beam inspection tools, and finds patterning defects down to 7 nm[7].
  • Film and shape metrology measures how thick each film is and how flat the wafer sits, without cutting it open. In this $2.6 billion family KLA held 45.6 percent, Nova 24.6 and Onto Innovation 10.9. Onto paid about $720 million in August 2026 for 27 percent of the Japanese X-ray tool maker Rigaku[8].
  • Mask inspection and repair has its own tools, because a defect on a mask, the stencil the circuit pattern is printed from, repeats on every die. This $2.2 billion family is one of two where KLA has a close rival. KLA held 45.9 percent, Lasertec 42 and Zeiss 10.1. Lasertec also makes actinic inspection tools, which check EUV masks with the same 13.5 nm light that prints them[9]. Lasertec calls its ACTIS A150 the world's first EUV patterned mask inspection system[9]. KLA's own actinic mask inspection tool was still at an early demo stage at its March 2026 investor day[3].
  • Overlay metrology measures whether this layer sits on the one below. Its $991.4 million market was split almost evenly between KLA at 51.5 percent and ASML at 47.9.
  • Critical dimension metrology, also called line-width measurement, measures how wide a printed feature came out. It is the one family Japan leads. Hitachi held 71.9 percent of this $1.2 billion market and Applied Materials 27.5.
  • Electron-beam metrology resolves detail too fine for light. Applied Materials led this $1.3 billion family at 45.1 percent, with ASML at 35.6 and KLA at 18.8.

Who makes it

KLA held 56.8 percent of a $15.7 billion market in 2025[1]. KLA says its share grew 3.6 percentage points from 2021 to 2025[4]. It says it gained share again in 2025 across mask, optical wafer and e-beam inspection[4]. Its revenue for fiscal 2026, the year to June 2026, was $13.579 billion, up from $12.156 billion in fiscal 2025[10].

The rest are specialists, and none holds more than 11.2 percent, by CSET's count for 2025[1].

  • Applied Materials is the largest of them at 11.2 percent. It sells e-beam defect review tools, CD-SEMs (electron microscopes that measure line width) and e-beam metrology tools next to the deposition and etch tools that create the defects.
  • Lasertec holds 6.4 percent, almost all of it mask inspection. Hitachi High-Tech holds 6.2 percent, most of it from CD-SEMs. ASML holds 5.9 percent through YieldStar overlay and HMI e-beam metrology.
  • Nova holds 4.3 percent, through film metrology, and took $880.6 million of revenue in 2025[11].
  • Onto Innovation holds 2.6 percent on $1,005.3 million of 2025 revenue[12]. Camtek holds 1.6 percent on $496.1 million of 2025 revenue[13].

KLA's patterning line, which includes several metrology products and mask inspection, grew 61 percent year on year in the June 2026 quarter[2]. In that quarter Taiwan took 31 percent of KLA's revenue and China 26 percent[2].

KLA says process control's share of fab spending is still rising[4]. In memory chips, KLA credits the rise to higher performance specifications, less redundancy (fewer spare circuits) and more logic content in devices built for high-performance computing[4].

KLA's systems analyze data with AI and also filter out noise[4]. In April 2026 KLA said it had added AI to every product line over the previous five years[4].

Packaging, AI and China

KLA says the AI build-out is making advanced packaging, and the process control it needs, more important[2]. KLA became the largest supplier of process control tools for advanced wafer-level packaging in 2025, adding 14 percentage points of share[4]. It expects about $1.1 billion of packaging process control revenue in 2026, up more than 70 percent[2]. Onto signed a volume purchase agreement estimated at over $240 million with an HBM maker for 2D inspection and 3D bump metrology through 2027[12].

Chinese makers are still small in process control, but one of them is growing fast. CSET's count, built on TechInsights data, puts all Chinese firms at 0.7 percent of a $15.7 billion market in 2025[1]. Skyverse (Shenzhen Zhongke Feice), a maker of wafer inspection and metrology tools, reported 2.05 billion yuan of revenue in 2025, about $285 million[14]. That was up 48.75 percent on 2024 and more than double its 2023 revenue[14]. Skyverse's revenue alone is about 1.8 percent of CSET's market, more than twice CSET's figure for all Chinese firms, so the CSET count may miss some domestic sales[1]. In its 2025 annual report Skyverse says Chinese makers still hold a low share of China's market for these tools and that KLA holds the largest share of it[14].

By CSET's 2025 count, Chinese firms held 0.6 percent of defect inspection tools[15]. They held 0.4 percent of line-width measurement tools in 2025[16]. In film and shape metrology they held 2 percent in 2025, all of it from Raintree Scientific Instruments, or RSIC[17]. They held no share of mask inspection and repair tools in 2025[18]. Nor did they hold any share that year of the tools that inspect wafers during advanced packaging[19].

In October 2022 the US began requiring a license for any US-made item, process control tools included, bound for certain Chinese fabs[20]. The rule covered fabs that made logic chips at 16/14 nm or below, NAND memory with 128 or more layers, or DRAM at 18 nm half-pitch or below[20].

A December 2024 rule added specific process control tools to the export control list. It controls tools for defect inspection and measurement of patterned 300 mm wafers if they can find defects of 21 nm or smaller[21]. They must do this using light with a wavelength below 400 nm, an electron beam resolving 1.65 nm, a cold field emission source, or two or more beams[21]. The same rule controls overlay metrology accurate to 0.5 nm or better if the tool is built into the track (the machine that coats and develops the light-sensitive resist) or can switch wavelengths quickly[21]. It also controls stand-alone wafer shape metrology that feeds corrections to immersion or EUV scanners[21]. A separate new entry, 3B994, covers optical film and line-width metrology for 300 mm wafers with software for measuring non-planar transistors[21].

BIS, the US Commerce Department bureau that wrote the rule, placed these tools in new entries for items it says also have legitimate uses in older chipmaking[21]. So they carry narrower license requirements than tools built only for advanced chips[21]. A new foreign direct product rule extends US jurisdiction to specified foreign-made chipmaking tools bound for Macau or for a Country Group D:5 destination such as China[22].

The chokepoint

One firm, KLA, held more than half the process control market in 2025. Several firms can build a good film metrology tool, but KLA leads most kinds of process control tool, and it says its share grew from 2021 to 2025. A fab that can buy scanners and etchers but not sensitive inspection tools finds fewer of the defects that lower its yield, so its yield rises more slowly.

Key evaluation criteria

  • Sensitivity. The smallest killer defect a tool can find. ASML's multibeam system is specified to 7 nm patterning defects[7].
  • Throughput. Wafers per hour, which sets how many lots a fab can afford to look at. ASML's multibeam system gives up to 15 times the throughput of single-beam tools[7].
  • Nuisance rate. The share of flagged events that turn out not to be real defects. AI classification is meant to reduce it.
  • Sampling plan. How many wafers in each lot the fab checks, and how many spots on each wafer. The plan sets what process control costs the fab, so it is a cost decision as well as a technical one.
  • Time to result. How fast a measurement reaches the process engineer, which sets the speed of yield learning.

Review questions

Open a question to see its answer.

What do metrology and inspection tools do?

They check each wafer between steps for line width, layer alignment and defects.

Their measurements tell a fab why its chips fail. Reread: How it works

Why do AI chips depend so much on finding defects?

They are among the largest chips made, and a bigger chip is more likely to have a defect.

On a chip that size, halving the defects raises the share of flawless chips from about half to about seven in ten. Reread: Packaging, AI and China

Who leads the market for these tools?

KLA, an American firm, with 56.8 percent of the market in 2025 on CSET's count.

That is about five times the share of Applied Materials, the next largest. KLA, citing Gartner, put its own 2024 share at 56.5 percent. Every kind of tool still has a second maker. Reread: Who makes it

How strong are Chinese makers of these tools?

Still small, though one of them is growing fast.

CSET counts Chinese makers at 0.7 percent of the market in 2025. Skyverse, a Shenzhen maker, reported 2025 revenue of 2.05 billion yuan, up 48.75 percent on 2024. That revenue alone is about 1.8 percent of the market, so CSET's count may miss some domestic sales. Reread: Packaging, AI and China
